title: Bruno Mars - Risk It All [Official Music Video]

source.title: Bruno Mars - Risk It All [Official Music Video]

review: M. Delacroix (a Parisian salon critic, 1842): I am pleased that the phrases close properly, with honest cadences; the voices move with propriety; the melody sits squarely on the beat. The melody is quite memorable – I find myself humming it.

layers.text: The vocal line is kept, but placed squarely on the beat and given period ornaments.
The bass is re-written as a period bass line (walking, Alberti or sustained).
The original backing is replaced by the composer's own accompaniment textures over (re-)harmonised chords.
No drums. Timpani only mark the big cadences, as in a real score.

song.title: Bruno Mars - Risk It All [Official Music Video]

era.name: Romantic
era.summary: Emotion first: long singing melodies, rich and colourful harmony, flexible tempo (rubato), big dynamic swells and larger orchestras.
traits: Rubato: tempo breathes, slowing at phrase ends
Wide piano arpeggios held by the sustain pedal
Richer chords: borrowed chords, diminished sevenths, chromatic colour
Huge dynamic range, from whisper to full orchestra
era.instruments: Grand piano, full string sections, clarinets, horns, harp, expanded brass and percussion
why: All three eras were tried. Romantic scored best (Romantic 1.163, Baroque 1.149, Classical 1.052). The score combines how classical it sounds, how much of the song survives, and how well the song suits the composer.
The vocal line is quite syncopated (17% of notes push across the beat). Romantic rubato and freer phrasing absorb that better than a strict Baroque or Classical pulse.
Some chords fall outside the plain key, which Romantic harmony welcomes.

composer.name: Johannes Brahms
composer.bio: Romantic warmth with Baroque craft: rich, autumnal textures, inner counter-melodies and the dark glow of clarinet and viola.
reasons: its moderate tempo (89 bpm) is right in Brahms's comfort zone
the wide-ranging vocal melody suits a composer known for long, singing lines
applied: Pulsing string chords, horns and harp swell under the melody in the loud sections

ensemble.name: Orchestra
ensemble.summary: String sections plus woodwinds, horns or trumpets, timpani (and harp in Romantic style).
why: It is one of Brahms's favourite settings.
In this composer's style it scored best of the four ensembles: Orchestra 1.163, Chamber ensemble 1.087, String quartet 1.078, Solo keyboard 1.055.
Why it works: the full colour palette: the song's loud choruses can swell into the whole orchestra.
The violins i carries the vocal melody (F#4–B5). It was moved by octaves into the instrument's most singing register, with the key unchanged.

changes.ending: It follows the original beat by beat and lasts exactly as long as the clip (19.1s).
changes.dropped: The drum kit, synths and electric bass are gone. Their rhythmic drive now comes from the accompaniment patterns.
